content: The Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis recommends the use of albendazole in combination with diethylcarbamazine (DEC) or ivermectin for mass drug administration. In areas where loiasis is endemic, albendazole alone is recommended. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of albendazole alone and in combination with DEC or ivermectin in individuals and communities affected by lymphatic filariasis. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, up to January 15, 2018. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster-RCTs were included if they compared albendazole to placebo or no treatment, or albendazole combined with a microfilaricidal drug to the microfilaricidal drug alone. The outcomes assessed included microfilariae (mf) prevalence and density, markers of adult worm infection (antigenaemia prevalence and density, adult worm prevalence detected by ultrasound), clinical disease, and adverse events. Thirteen trials were included in the analysis, involving a total of 8713 participants. Of these, 12 were individually randomized trials, and one was a small cluster-randomized trial. None of the trials evaluated the population-level effects of albendazole in mass drug administration programs. Seven trials enrolled individuals with specific filarial infection criteria, while six trials included participants from endemic areas. Outcomes were reported as either end values or changes from baseline. Mf and antigen density data were presented using geometric means, log means, or arithmetic means, with reductions in density calculated in various ways. For mf prevalence over a period of two weeks to 12 months, albendazole alone or in combination with another microfilaricidal drug showed little to no difference compared to controls (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.07; 5027 participants, 12 trials, high-certainty evidence). Regarding mf density, the results were inconsistent, with some trials showing greater reductions in the albendazole group and others in the control group. For mf density at six months and 12 months, the evidence was of very low certainty, and it remains unclear whether albendazole has any effect. For antigenaemia prevalence between six and 12 months, albendazole alone or in combination with another microfilaricidal drug showed little to no difference (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.12; 3774 participants, 7 trials, high-certainty evidence). Similarly, for antigen density over the same period, there was little to no effect, but the evidence was of very low certainty (1374 participants, 5 trials). For adult worm prevalence detected by ultrasound at 12 months, albendazole combined with a microfilaricidal drug may make little to no difference (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.86; 165 participants, 3 trials, low-certainty evidence). Adverse events reported by participants showed no significant difference between those receiving albendazole and those in the control group (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.13; 2894 participants, 6 trials, high-certainty evidence). Meta-analyses and GRADE tables were also provided for specific comparisons: albendazole versus placebo (4 trials, 1870 participants), albendazole with DEC versus DEC alone (8 trials, 3405 participants), and albendazole with ivermectin versus ivermectin alone (4 trials, 3438 participants). In conclusion, the evidence suggests that albendazole has little impact on clearing microfilaraemia or adult filarial worms within 12 months of treatment. This finding is consistent across trials evaluating albendazole alone or in combination with DEC or ivermectin. The trials assessing mf density involved small sample sizes, used varying methods to calculate density, and produced inconsistent results. These findings raise questions about the role of albendazole in the elimination of lymphatic filariasis. For areas where loiasis is endemic and only albendazole can be used, placebo-controlled trials of albendazole alone may be warranted to inform policy decisions.
